extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in sociology, media studies, criminology and policing; scholars interested in moral panic and crime reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying how media, police and judicial practices construct and amplify a 'moral panic' (here, the 'mugging' panic), including the role of labeling, statistical claims, courtroom ritual, and transnational imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty as a news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a conventional news value; the press may invent a whole new category in order to catch public attention with 'something new and different'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues press will present or frame phenomena as 'novel' even when the facts are not new; this framing helps justify heightened coverage and public alarm. Anti-pattern: treating an ordinary set of crimes as a newly emergent phenomenon without corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling and ideological recategorisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The label helped to break up and recategorise the general field of crime - the ideological frame which it laid across the field of social vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a new label (e.g. 'mugging') can restructure how diverse incidents are perceived, turning disparate events into a single social problem. Guidance: examine how a label groups events and what boundaries it creates; beware of redefinition that obscures prior categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical basis and evidential robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistical basis to this reconstruction of events does not stand up well under scrutiny; the reaction to 'mugging' was out of all proportion to any level of actual threat which could be reconstructed through the unreliable statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of a crime 'wave' by checking the reliability and interpretation of statistics. Anti-pattern: accepting headline crime counts or selective figures without assessing comparators, denominators, or reporting biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media responsibility for relaying dominant definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the public has little direct experience of crime, the media must bear some responsibility for relaying the dominant definition of mugging to the public at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how media choice of frames, sources, and language transmits an authoritative definition; check whether alternative voices or contexts are given. Example: dominance of court reports and judges' comments shaped public understanding more than event reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transnational framing / 'special relationship' import
rubrics_metrics.description: The slow translation of 'mugging' from its American setting to British ground was shaped by a 'special relationship' between the media in Britain and the United States; American experience provided the label and its field of associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating domestic coverage, note whether foreign cases or imagery are used as templates or warnings ('Will Harlem come to Handsworth?') and whether time-lag/anticipation arguments are deployed to justify pre-emptive policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative embedding in linked frames
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Mugging' was embedded in a number of linked frames: the race conflict; the urban crisis; rising crime; the breakdown of 'law and order'; the liberal conspiracy; the white backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the broader social themes and cultural narratives that a label carries with it; these associations amplify emotional responses. Anti-pattern: using a label without unpacking its loaded connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalisation and pre-sensationalised imports
rubrics_metrics.description: The label arrived in Britain already established in its most sensational and sensationalised form; this pre-history helped trigger its own sensational spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for imported frames that are already dramatized; such sensationalisation predisposes media and public to escalate concerns immediately. Example: American coverage made British uptake alarmist from inception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexical use of labels as shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is indexical: simply by using the label, a whole social history of the contemporary United States can be immediately and graphically mapped into place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the implications whenever a shorthand label is used — it summons a bundle of meanings beyond the immediate facts. Guidance: require explication rather than relying on indexical shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege of court reports over event reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Court reports, especially on the day of sentencing and where judges' summing-up are quoted, get fuller, longer, more dramatic treatment and are more prominently positioned than event reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how media preference for courtroom rhetoric amplifies the perceived severity and moral dimensions of crime; tracking shifts from event coverage to court coverage can indicate the peak of a moral panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial homilies as definitional performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges' closing speeches and homilies allowed the judiciary to define and structure the public definition of 'mugging' and the 'wave of muggings' in particular; their uniform language produced a 'consensus of judges'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider judicial rhetoric not merely as legal procedure but as a public performative that the media relays; these speeches justify harsher sentences and shape public perception. Anti-pattern: treating judicial remarks as neutral legal fact rather than ideological input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of counter-definitions/voices
rubrics_metrics.description: The consensus of judges was rendered more persuasive by the lack of counter-definitions; defence counsels, defendants and sympathetic voices were conspicuously absent from coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media narratives, check for silenced or marginalized perspectives; the absence of counter-narratives facilitates a one-sided moral panic. Example: very few interviews with alleged muggers were published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-existing social anxieties as fertile ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The soil of judicial and social reaction was already well tilled in preparation for its timely and long-prepared advent; pre-existing anxieties (about permissiveness, race, urban decay) made certain frames effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether current reportage taps into pre-existing fears or narratives — these make moral panics more likely and more intense. Anti-pattern: assuming panic arises de novo from isolated incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of media and state control apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The media's key role cannot be treated in isolation; it must be analysed together with other collective agencies in the 'mugging' drama—the central apparatus of social control in the state: the police and the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news coverage by tracing source networks and institutional alliances (police, transport anti-mugging squads, courts) that produce, legitimise and amplify definitions. Example: police and judges gave cues that the press followed and amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual enactment and newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremonial ritual act of the judge (admonitions, denunciations) is as much the occasion for media interest as the crime itself; ritual degradation helps constitute the moral panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how ritualized institutional acts (sentencing rituals, public admonitions) are used by media as narrative fulcrums to dramatize social threats. Indicator: prominent headlines and long quotations from judicial ritual speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-markers in coverage (events vs court cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in the press coverage of 'mugging' from 'events' to 'court cases', and later back to 'events only', were not random: the first marks the 'peak'; the second the decline in the 'moral panic' itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes in the type of coverage (event-focused vs court-focused) as a diagnostic of where a moral panic sits on its lifecycle. Guidance: chart proportions and prominence of each type over time.
